newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian govt, unions grapple with pensions reform.
newsitem.headline: Italian govt, unions grapple with pensions reform.

text.p: The Italian government, trying to slash its bloated pensions bill by five trillion lire ($3 billion), met union leaders on Tuesday for the first round of detailed talks on overhauling the creaking system.
The meeting, between ministers and leaders of the three big trade union confederations, took place in a "positive atmosphere on both sides," Labour Minister Tiziano Treu said.
"There's a willingness to discuss possible solutions...It was a useful meeting but an overview," he told reporters.

Most of the morning meeting was taken up deciding what the negotiations should actually be about. "Before we talk about pensions we have to agree on what comes under pensions and what comes under social security," he said.
Sergio Cofferati, leader of the biggest union confederation, Cgil, said there was still a long way to go.
"We and the government have different ways of evaluating what is social security and what is pension spending," he said.

Italy's centre-left government formally opened talks with union leaders and employers' groups a month ago to hammer out lasting reform to a cash-guzzling system that analysts say needs urgent attention if Italy is to join Europe's single currency.

The government, which was scheduled to hold bilateral talks with employers' group Confindustria later on Tuesday, wants to make it harder to qualify for length-of-service pensions which are proving one of the biggest drains on the system.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi has questioned whether the country can afford the early retirement system that allows Italians to draw a pension based on length of service rather than their age.
Some 52,000 more Italians than expected claimed early retirement pensions in the first four months of 1997, according to financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore.
The paper said a high proportion of the claimants were civil servants.
